title: Decision scenario
body: A customer's order has not arrived. Work through the call - each choice leads somewhere different.
instruction: Read the situation and choose a response to see what happens next.
ariaRegion: Decision scenario. Read each situation and choose a response to see what happens next.

s1.body: A client calls because their order has not arrived. They sound annoyed. How do you respond?

_choices.text: Apologise and promise a same-day redelivery.
_choices.consequence: The client calms down - but you have not checked whether same-day delivery is even possible.

_choices.text: Ask for the order number and check what happened.
_choices.consequence: You get the facts before acting. A steady start.

_choices.text: Explain that deliveries are handled by another team.
_choices.consequence: The client feels passed around, and more frustrated than before.

s2.body: You check and find same-day delivery is not possible. The client is now expecting it. What now?

_choices.text: Call back and explain the delay honestly.
_choices.consequence: Awkward, but being straight starts to rebuild trust.

_choices.text: Send a standard email and hope they do not call.
_choices.consequence: They call back - angrier - and it becomes a complaint.

s3.body: You find the parcel is delayed in transit and will arrive tomorrow. What do you tell the client?

_choices.text: Give the real delivery date and offer a small goodwill gesture.
Tell them it is 'on its way' without a date.
_choices.consequence: Vague reassurance - they are likely to call again.

good.body: The client thanks you. You kept them informed and set a realistic expectation - that is what rebuilds trust after a slip.

neutral.body: The issue is resolved, but the client is left unsure. A clear delivery date would have closed it properly.

poor.body: The call escalates into a formal complaint. The lesson: check the facts and set honest expectations before you promise anything.

title: The practice as one cycle
body: Writing as a member of your discipline works as one continuing cycle, repeated each time you write. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Recognise
_items.body: Recognise that your field sets its own conventions, rather than following one universal standard.

_items.title: Read
_items.body: Read published work in your field as a writer, not only as a reader, to learn those conventions.

_items.title: Draft
_items.body: Draft in those conventions, using sources with a critical edge so they serve your own argument.

_items.title: Check and carry
_items.body: Check your writing against the work you admire, and carry what you learn into the next piece, so the cycle turns again.

title: Explore the concept
body: Four moves that take you from a task to a first draft. Open each to see the step.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Read the steer
_items.body: The steer is the instruction word in the task: analyse, discuss, compare, evaluate. It tells you what kind of thinking the question wants. 'Describe' and 'evaluate' ask for very different essays, so the steer shapes everything that follows.

_items.title: Find the keywords
_items.body: The keywords fix the topic and its limits: the specific terms, the time period, the place, the scope. Underlining them stops you writing a good essay on the wrong question, a common and costly mistake.

_items.title: Make a rough plan
_items.body: A plan is a short map of your main points and the order they come in. It does not need to be neat. Its job is to turn a vague sense of what you want to say into a shape you can write to.

_items.title: Get a draft down
_items.body: With a plan in front of you, write a quick first draft that follows it. Do not stop to perfect sentences. The aim is a complete rough version you can then improve, not a finished paragraph you are afraid to change.

title: A prompting session, move by move
displayTitle: A prompting session, move by move
body: A good session is a dialogue, not one question. Open each move to see how it builds on the last.
instruction: Open any move to read it. You can keep more than one open at once.

_items.title: Move 1: Open with a framed prompt
_items.body: Set a role, a clear task and your context, then send your first prompt.
_items.advice: In practice: name who the AI should be, what you want it to do, and your level and module. A framed prompt earns a sharper first answer.

_items.title: Move 2: Ask for the method
_items.body: Ask the AI to show the steps or the reasoning, not just the final answer.
_items.advice: In practice: add "show me how to work it out, do not just give the answer". You learn the method, and you can check each step.

_items.title: Move 3: Push back
_items.body: Challenge a weak point, or ask the AI to critique its own answer.
_items.advice: In practice: try "what is the weakest part of that?" or "give me the counter-argument". Pushing back surfaces gaps and deepens the dialogue.

_items.title: Move 4: Apply it yourself
_items.body: Close the tool and redo the task in your own words to check you have learnt it.
_items.advice: In practice: the real test is what you can do with the tool closed. If you cannot, go back a move and work it through again.

title: Formative check: no single academic writing
displayTitle: Why is it misleading to talk about 'academic writing' as a single skill?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it misleading to treat academic writing as a single skill?

_items.text: Because each discipline sets its own conventions for style, vocabulary and structure.
_items.feedback: Yes. Writing is situated in a field, and its conventions are local to that field.

_items.text: Because some students write well and others do not, whatever the subject.
_items.feedback: The point is not about individual ability; it is that conventions differ by field.

_items.text: Because academic writing is really just the same as good writing in general.
_items.feedback: That is the assumption the lesson rejects: there is no single standard above every subject.

_items.text: Because only the sciences have strict rules for writing.
_items.feedback: Every discipline has conventions, not only the sciences; they simply differ.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Academic writing is not monolithic: each field sets its own conventions.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what varies between a chemist's writing and a historian's.
_incorrect.final: Academic writing is not one skill because each discipline sets its own conventions for style, vocabulary and structure.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The basics of a good revision
body: Four parts of revising a draft. Select each tab to see what it asks you to do.
instruction: Select each tab to read about that part.

_items.title: Structure
_items.body: Structure is the order your points come in and how they connect. At the macro level it is the overall arrangement of the whole piece; at the micro level it is how each paragraph opens and links to the next. A reader should always be able to see what a paragraph is about and how it follows on.

_items.title: Clarity
_items.body: Clarity is writing a reader understands first time. A reliable move is the subject-verb-object sentence: say who did what to what, in that order. Using the active voice ('the owner locked the door') rather than the passive ('the door was locked') usually gives a sentence more impact and leaves less to guess.

_items.title: Editing
_items.body: Editing is where the real improvement happens. It means deleting text, adding it, changing how you express things, and creating new paragraphs. It works on the substance and shape of the writing, not just its surface, and it is worth far more than a quick read-through.

_items.title: Proofreading
_items.body: Proofreading comes last. It is polishing the text: eliminating typos and the superficial errors that are easy to correct once the writing itself is settled. It is not the same as editing, and doing only this is why many drafts still read poorly.

title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about writing as a member of your discipline. By now you can work through the writing process and get a draft structured and clear. The step this course takes is different. It treats academic writing not as one universal skill but as a practice shaped by the field you write in.

By the end you will be able to explain how writing conventions vary across disciplines and characterise your own, appraise published writing to work out its conventions, and integrate sources with a critical edge so that your writing advances an argument of your own.
